name: French Winawer, Poisoned Pawn
summary: The Winawer Poisoned Pawn (C18) sees Black allow Qxg7 after 7...Qc7, sacrificing kingside pawns for fast development and pressure on White's weak c3 and d4.
intro: The Winawer Poisoned Pawn is the main-line battleground of the French Winawer, reached after 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3 Bxc3+ 6.bxc3 Ne7 7.Qg4 Qc7. White's queen sortie hits g7, and rather than defend, Black offers the pawn: after 8.Qxg7 Rg8 9.Qxh7 White snatches two kingside pawns while Black seizes a huge lead in development and hammers away at White's shattered c3 and d4 pawns down the open g- and c-files. The result is one of the most deeply analysed and double-edged pawn sacrifices in all of chess, where a single tempo can decide whether White's extra material or Black's initiative prevails.

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The Poisoned Pawn crystallises the Winawer's clash of assets in its sharpest form. White has the bishop pair, a broad pawn front and, after grabbing on g7 and h7, two extra kingside pawns. Black has surrendered the dark-squared bishop but gained a commanding lead in development, open g- and c-files, and a fixed target in White's doubled, isolated c-pawns. The whole struggle becomes a race: can Black's pieces generate a decisive initiative against White's uncastled king and fragile centre before the extra pawns and bishops begin to tell?

Concrete factors dominate over general principles. White's king is often stuck in the centre, so Black rushes rooks to the open files, plays ...Nbc6 and ...Bd7 with ...O-O-O, and looks to break with ...d4 or land a knight on f5. White, for their part, tries to consolidate, return some material at the right moment, blunt the initiative with timely trades, and steer toward an endgame where the two bishops and the healthier kingside majority outweigh the ruined queenside pawns.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The tabiya is set by 6...Ne7 7.Qg4 Qc7, defending g7 with the queen while inviting White to take it. After 8.Qxg7 Rg8 9.Qxh7 cxd4 the position explodes; a principal line runs 10.Ne2 Nbc6 11.f4, when Black continues with ...Bd7, ...dxc3 and ...O-O-O, throwing every piece at White's centre and king. The daring 10.Kd1, tucking the king away by hand, is a well-known alternative that keeps the extra pawns while accepting a lasting lag in development.

Black is not obliged to enter the pawn grab. The restrained 7...O-O invites White to attack with 8.Bd3 and h4-h5 but keeps the king safe behind the ...Ne7-f5 blockade, while 7...Kf8 sidesteps the capture on g7 altogether at the cost of castling rights. In every branch the recurring themes are the same: White's kingside pawn-storm and bishop pair against Black's pressure on c3, the ...d4 break, and the initiative that a lead in development provides.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Poisoned Pawn grew out of the broader Winawer, named for the nineteenth-century Polish master Szymon Winawer, but its razor-sharp main line became a proving ground for twentieth-century theory. Generations of grandmasters, from Mikhail Botvinnik to modern computer-armed analysts, have poured effort into the position after 9.Qxh7, and its evaluation has swung back and forth as new resources are discovered. It endures as one of the most heavily analysed pawn sacrifices in chess, a favourite of players who thrive in concrete, forcing, deeply theoretical battles.
